pr_title: py/objstr.c: Enforce unicode-safety when creating str from vstr.
pr_body:
Fixes #9044 and https://github.com/adafruit/circuitpython/issues/6752 (@jepler @RetiredWizard).

Rather than just ensuring that streams are unicode safe, this ensures that all usages of mp_obj_str_from_vstr are safe, as there are other ways to trigger this bug (see https://github.com/micropython/micropython/issues/9044#issuecomment-1218053443).

By changing the `*_from_vstr` API slightly, it's possible to do this in a way that overall reduces code size and comes in at -104 bytes on PYBV11.

I hope this isn't a huge breaking change for anyone writing user c modules (or for CircuitPython to merge) but it's a very straightforward find-and-replace to fix.
pr_comments: LGTM. Should we add a test, e.g. reading a file or memory stream with bad UTF-8 data?
What about calls to `mp_obj_new_str()` and `mp_obj_new_str_of_type()`?  Do they also need to validate?
Hi, thanks for making this PR. I look forward to replacing the quick patch in CircuitPython with it down the road, especially if some flash space is freed in the process.

I've added an optimised path `mp_obj_new_str_from_vstr_safe` for the cases outlined above (and one more in persistentcode.c).

> Should we add a test, e.g. reading a file or memory stream with bad UTF-8 data?

Good idea. Done.

> What about calls to `mp_obj_new_str()` and `mp_obj_new_str_of_type()`? Do they also need to validate?

I think the the former should always check (all the uses I could find were small strings or untrusted). I have added a commit to do this.

`mp_obj_new_str_of_type` calls `mp_obj_new_str`.

The other two interesting ones are:

`mp_obj_new_str_copy` -- this is always used on safe strings
`mp_obj_new_str_via_qstr` -- this is also always used on safe strings

I have added/updated the comments for both to state this as a requirement.

---

This now comes in at -72 bytes on PYBV11.
In `mp_obj_str_make_new` there are two calls to `utf8_check`.  I think the second can be removed, and I think the first needs to stay.

> In `mp_obj_str_make_new` there are two calls to `utf8_check`. I think the second can be removed, and I think the first needs to stay.

Yes good catch. Updated.

Now at -80 bytes.
Thanks for updating (and I also updated the code comment as per above).  Rebased and merged in 8a0ee5a5c04e83f04d1c62029ac5ba7c74856507 through bd4e45fd68e20af3f965b403e643fa5f71aa1b08
I also run the performance benchmarks before/after this PR, on PYBv1.0.  It was basically unchanged (as expected because there aren't any tests for string operations).

issue_context.title: various ways to read() don't check for valid utf-8, weirdness ensues
issue_context.body:
[Initial comment heavily revised because the original was unclear. Apologies if this breaks any of the context of the replies below]

Over in https://github.com/adafruit/circuitpython/issues/6752 a user reported that various ways to read from files didn't actually validate that the content was utf-8. Instead, it blithely stores the data in a `str`, which in Micropython must always be a valid utf-8 encoded chunk of memory.

This leads to weird behavior, such as when the file with the byte content `\xf7` is read:
```python
>>> with open("notutf8.txt", "rt", -1, "utf-8") as f: content = f.read()
... 
>>> f
<io.TextIOWrapper -1>
>>> content
'\x07'
>>> content[0]
'\x07\x00\x00\x00'
>>> 
```

The behavior is the same no matter what coding is specified, or if no coding is explicitly specified. As discussed below, it does not appear to be explicit anywhere that the encoding of a text file is utf-8. It is implicit in the way that reading a file with UTF-8 content works, and reading a file with non-UTF8 content yields up dragons.

I prepared a possible fix relative to CircuitPython at https://github.com/adafruit/circuitpython/pull/6754 -- is there interest in changing this behavior in micropython? if so, I can prepare a PR for y'all including hopefully adding tests.

basically, each code path in file reading will now check that the content is valid utf-8 in the case that a str, rather than a bytes, is being produced.
comments: IMHO it is not valid to assume that a file content always has to be utf-8 encoded. It may be anything. So such a check would only be reasonable if the file is opened requiring a specific encoding, like utf-8.

My interpretation of https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open is that by not specifying an encoding to `open()` we get the default encoding. We only support one encoding, so it makes sense that we're implicitly opening the file in utf-8 mode, and as such it does make sense that we should be doing the validation if it's a text-mode stream.

Weird stuff starts happening when a str object has non-utf8 content. The original poster over in circuitpython found, for instance, that this value doesn't subscript right ... here, "notutf8.txt" contains the single byte \xf7:
```
>>> with open("notutf8.txt") as f: content = f.read()
... 
>>> content
'\x07'
>>> content[0]
'\x07\x00\x00\x00'
>>> ord(content[0])
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: ord() expected a character, but string of length 4 found
```

stopping weirdness like this "at the source" will hopefully save somebody time down the line, too.
Doesn't the documentation say that the default of the parameter encoding is None = No encoding? And obviously that applies only to text files.

The CPython documentation says:

>  In text mode, if encoding is not specified the encoding used is platform-dependent: locale.getpreferredencoding(False) is called to get the current locale encoding. 

The MicroPython documentation does say anything about it, AFAICT.
So for MicroPython the default encoding is: No encoding.

> So for MicroPython the default encoding is: No encoding.

What would it mean for there to be "no encoding" for a file opened in text mode?

MicroPython's default (and only) encoding is "utf-8". To illustrate this, if I write a file out to the filesystem containing utf-8 encoded data, then read it back in with the default options, it is interpreted as utf-8. If there was no encoding, then no interpretation of the `\xe2...` into the single unicode character `\u2b50` (i.e. ⭐) would have happened.

```
MicroPython v1.19.1-290-ga1a5a6539 on 2022-08-17; PYBv1.1 with STM32F405RG
Type "help()" for more information.
>>> f = open('data', 'wb')
>>> f.write(b'hello \xe2\xad\x90 world')
15
>>> f.close()
>>>
>>> f = open('data', 'r')
>>> f.read()
'hello \u2b50 world'
>>> _[6]
'\u2b50'
>>> len(_)
1
>>> f.close()
```

In Python (and MicroPython) a (utf-8) string that appears to contain `\xe2` for example, is actually encoded as `b'\xc3\xa2'`
See https://www.utf8-chartable.de/unicode-utf8-table.pl?start=128&number=128&utf8=string-literal&unicodeinhtml=hex

```
>>> s = 'hello \xe2\xad\x90 world'   # Will be stored internally as utf-8: \xe2 -> \xc3a2
>>> s[6]  # string substring understands the encoding
'\xe2'
>>> uctypes.bytes_at(uctypes.addressof(s), 18)    # no conversion, just get the raw bytes for this object
b'hello \xc3\xa2\xc2\xad\xc2\x90 world'
```

@jepler I think your fix makes sense, but I perhaps it should be more general than just for `stream.c`.

i.e. be stricter about this and make `mp_obj_new_str_from_vstr` itself always do `utf8_check` (conditional on `MICROPY_PY_BUILTINS_STR_UNICODE_CHECK`). i.e. any method that creates or modifies a `str` object should maintain the invariant that the string is utf-8, and it should be impossible to create an invalid string.

Note that `mp_obj_str_make_new` already does this (which is why `bytes.decode` will catch this). But for example `mp_obj_new_str` and `mp_obj_new_str_copy` don't.

As an optimisation, in many cases `mp_obj_new_str_from_vstr`, `mp_obj_new_str`, and `mp_obj_new_str_copy` are working with data from already-valid string objects. Perhaps we should make those three methods always check, but then add `_safe` versions for places where you know you have valid data (which would likely be static/private to objstr.c).

```c
STATIC mp_obj_t mp_obj_new_str_copy_safe(const mp_obj_type_t *type, const byte *data, size_t len) {
}
mp_obj_t mp_obj_new_str_copy(const mp_obj_type_t *type, const byte *data, size_t len) {
    #if MICROPY_PY_BUILTINS_STR_UNICODE_CHECK
    if (!utf8_check(str_data, str_len)) {
        mp_raise_msg(&mp_type_UnicodeError, NULL);
    }
    #endif
    return mp_obj_new_str_copy_safe(type, data, len);
}
```

It was easy to find an example of being able to create an invalid string due to `mp_obj_new_str` being used incorrectly, e.g. on Pico W via using `sta_if.config(ssid=b'..invalid utf8 encoding..')` then reading it back with `sta_if.config('ssid')`.

review_comments:
Would be interesting to find a test case where doing a re match does raise a unicode error, and then check how CPython handles it.

Also, to reduce code size, maybe a helper like `mp_obj_new_str_type_from_vstr_checked(type, vstr)` could be added?
Can a filesystem have invalid chars in it?  How do you get the cwd if it does?  How does CPython handle this?
